case_study_insert.main_stem: Embers and Oak Restaurant Group (EORG) is a private limited company in the hospitality and restaurant sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2013 by Meera Kapoor, the group runs four casual-dining restaurants in regional cities and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership, where restaurant managers vote on menu changes. EORG plans to invest $750,000 in launching a franchise programme for its flagship brand, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $2,100,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $24.50, and currently produces 260,000 units a year (one unit is one meal served). EORG faces two problems: two head chefs were poached by a rival chain in October 2026, and kitchen absenteeism stands at 12%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Advertisement Extract — Weekend Herald, November 2026: 'Embers and Oak — family dining from $14.90 a head; two-for-one mains on Tuesdays; free children's dessert on Sundays; loyalty card gives 10% off every fifth visit.' Operations note: the four restaurants served 62,400 covers in Q3 2026, average spend was $31.60 per cover, food-waste rate is 6.8%, and 78% of 500 surveyed diners rated the group 'very good'; repeat visits account for 57% of trade. The food-cost complaint rate is 2.1%, down from 3.4% a year ago.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Embers and Oak Restaurant Group as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.5% to 6.25%, lifting borrowing costs for restaurant expansion. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $10.40 to $11.05 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for front-of-house and kitchen staff. (3) Wholesale protein, dairy and fresh produce prices have risen 10.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on dining out grew 2.9% in the same period.

questions.question_text: EORG plans to finance part of its franchise programme launch with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for EORG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs EORG nothing in interest, which matters because wholesale protein, dairy and fresh produce prices have already risen 10.6% and eating-out inflation pressures diners; EORG's $2,100,000 fixed costs and the $450,000 bank loan commitment would otherwise squeeze the margin on its $24.50 average selling price even faster. Keeping the franchise launch interest-free preserves cash for marketing the flagship brand and for absorbing the $31.60 average cover spend that keeps repeat visits at 57% of trade.

Point 2: Using $300,000 of retained profit avoids collateral and lender conditions on the franchise programme, so Meera Kapoor and the four restaurant managers retain full control over brand standards, franchise fees and menu voting decisions. It also leaves borrowing capacity unused, which is valuable given the base interest rate just rose to 6.25% and EORG may need faster, flexible funding later if the first franchised sites underperform or if poached head chefs need replacing urgently.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Embers and Oak Restaurant Group and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: EORG is launching its franchise programme for the flagship brand. Consider national television advertising, print advertising in weekend newspaper supplements, or social media influencer marketing. Which should EORG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would give EORG the fastest, widest awareness of the franchise opportunity, reaching entrepreneurs and potential franchisees nationwide and lending the group a trustworthy, established image. However, production and airtime are very expensive for four restaurants and 120 employees financing $750,000 of expansion partly on a $450,000 bank loan, and much of a national audience is not a prospective franchisee or regular diner at $31.60 per cover; coverage waste would be high.

Print advertising in weekend supplements: Weekend titles reach an affluent, food-interested readership, suit detailed franchise-opportunity storytelling with founder Meera Kapoor's narrative, and match EORG's existing 'Weekend Herald' presence (the two-for-one Tuesdays and loyalty card offer already in the insert). Print is cheaper than TV but still costly per response, and readership skew older, missing younger franchise candidates and younger diners who drive Tuesday two-for-one trade.

Social media influencer marketing: Food-influencer partnerships show the dining experience authentically video-first, target the 78% of surveyed diners rating the group 'very good', cost far less than TV, and can be measured precisely through bookings, loyalty-card sign-ups and franchise enquiries. Credibility risk exists if an influencer misrepresents the brand, but alignment with food creators who genuinely rate Embers and Oak is inexpensive and highly targeted.

Recommendation: EORG should choose social media influencer marketing. It proves the brand visually to exactly the diners and franchise prospects most likely to convert, leverages the 57% repeat-visit base and 2.1% complaint rate down-trend, and fits a $750,000 programme without exhausting the $450,000 bank loan. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable; print supplements are rejected as too narrow and older-skewing for franchise recruitment, though EORG should keep targeted print for franchise-opportunity sections where serious investors read.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of EORG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of EORG with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and print are rejected.

questions.question_text: EORG's two head chefs were poached by a rival chain and kitchen absenteeism stands at 12%. Explain two benefits for EORG of introducing a profit-sharing scheme for its kitchen teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Profit sharing gives kitchen teams a direct financial stake in the group's success, raising motivation exactly where EORG needs it most — after losing two head chefs to a rival. Staff who share profits think like owners: they control portion waste (the food-waste rate is 6.8%), police prep standards and support each other through service, reducing the desperation to defect to the rival's higher salaries and tackling the 12% kitchen absenteeism caused by disengagement.

Point 2: Profit sharing aligns the four restaurants behind shared goals, reinforcing the hierarchical-yet-democratic structure by rewarding managers democratically and kitchen crews collectively. It is cheaper than across-the-board wage rises amid the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $11.05 and the 10.6% food inflation, yet it binds key staff to the franchise plan: ambitious cooks see a bonus future inside EORG rather than leaving, which protects the 57% repeat-diner base and the $31.60 average spend that franchisee recruits will be buying into.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to EORG's poaching problem, absenteeism and franchise plans.

questions.question_text: EORG must appoint a training manager to run the franchise training programme. Consider recruiting an experienced external franchise trainer or promoting an existing senior sous-chef and giving them off-the-job training. Which should EORG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Experienced external franchise trainer: An outside trainer brings proven systems, franchise-audit experience and immediate credibility with prospective franchisees, accelerating the programme's launch and producing consistent brand-standard manuals from day one. Their salary would command a premium, and they would not know EORG's kitchen culture, the two-for-one Tuesday mechanics or the 6.8% waste problem without a handover period; there is also a risk they impose off-the-shelf franchise models that do not fit casual dining.

Promoting an existing senior sous-chef: An internal promotion rewards loyalty after the October poaching crisis, preserves kitchen authenticity and EORG's democratic menu culture, and signals to every cook that advancement exists inside the group. The cost is much lower, and the off-the-job training investment is recoverable if they succeed; the risks are a temporary leadership gap in their kitchen, and slower credibility with franchisees who expect formal franchise experience.

Decision: EORG should choose promoting an existing senior sous-chef with structured off-the-job training. It is cheaper than the external salary premium, heals the morale damage from poaching, and keeps the franchise brand culinary-authentic — decisive for convincing franchisees that the flagship experience is replicable. The external hire is rejected because EORG's margin cannot carry an external salary premium while $450,000 of bank loan is outstanding; if the promoted sous-chef lacks franchising audit skills after training, EORG can hire an external consultant part-time instead of a full-time replacement. Meera Kapoor should also publish the selection criteria to all kitchen teams within a week of the decision, rebuilding trust after October's poaching and showing every cook that advancement exists inside Embers and Oak.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two appointment options with limited application to EORG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of EORG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of EORG with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture, capability and franchise credibility.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how EORG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $2,100,000 ÷ ($24.50 − $9.50) = $2,100,000 ÷ $15.00 = 140,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 140,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $24.50 − $9.50 = $15.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways EORG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. EORG can compare the 140,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 260,000 meals, a margin of safety of 120,000 units, to confirm the four restaurants trade comfortably above break-even and can absorb the $450,000 bank loan repayments and 10.6% food inflation without cutting hours or quality.
2. With $15.00 contribution per meal, management can test the two-for-one Tuesday effect: promotions effectively halve price on those meals, so managers can model how many extra covers the offer must generate (at least double normal Tuesday volume) to keep total contribution above the $2,100,000 fixed-cost requirement.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution lets EORG set the royalty and fee structure for franchisees so that both parties cover their break-even, protecting brand consistency in the franchise programme funded by the $750,000 launch investment.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($2,100,000 ÷ 260,000 units + $9.50 = $17.58 a unit) to benchmark each restaurant, identify where the 6.8% food waste is concentrated, and decide whether to renegotiate supplier contracts amid 10.6% input inflation or adjust the $14.90 family-dining entry price to defend the 57% repeat trade.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 140,000 units a year, computed as $2,100,000 fixed costs divided by $15.00 contribution per meal (selling price $24.50 less variable cost $9.50). At the current 260,000 meals, EORG operates a margin of safety of 120,000 units, confirming the four restaurants trade deeply above break-even ahead of the franchise launch. (ii) Contribution per unit = $15.00 per meal served, the amount every meal adds toward fixed costs and then profit. (iii) Four applied uses: first, confirming the margin of safety can absorb the $450,000 bank loan while the flagship brand is franchised to new cities; second, modelling two-for-one Tuesdays where halved pricing must at least double covers to hold total contribution; third, setting franchise royalty and fee structures so franchisees also clear their own break-even after the $750,000 programme investment; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $17.58 per meal ($2,100,000 ÷ 260,000 + $9.50) to target the 6.8% food-waste rate driving margin erosion amid 10.6% input inflation. Together these uses let Meera Kapoor test every menu, promotion and franchise proposal against the fixed-cost base before capital is committed.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate EORG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has EORG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.21 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.94 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $315,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $170,000 + $120,000 = $400,000. Current liabilities rose from $260,000 to $310,000. 2024: $315,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.21; 2025: $400,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.29. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($315,000 − $95,000) ÷ $260,000 = $220,000 ÷ $260,000 = 0.85; 2025 = ($400,000 − $110,000) ÷ $310,000 = $290,000 ÷ $310,000 = 0.94.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened but remains tight. The headline cover improved only from 1.21 to 1.29 and both readings sit close to the 1.0 prudence zone, while current liabilities climbed from $260,000 to $310,000 — likely supplier credit and the growing cost of fresh produce during the 10.6% food-price surge. The stricter measure, though below 1.0 in both years, improved from 0.85 to 0.94, showing less reliance on selling stock to pay debts; inventories rose to $110,000, which is sensible for a growing group but ties up cash. Trade receivables rose to $170,000 — mostly corporate catering and franchise set-up fees — so collection discipline is now essential.

Conclusion: EORG's financial position has improved, but only modestly. Both measures moved in the right direction, cash rose to $120,000 and inventories are working, yet neither year shows comfortable cover and the stricter measure remains under 1.0. EORG should collect receivables aggressively, hold supplier payments as negotiated, and avoid drawing more than its $450,000 bank loan before the franchise royalty income materialises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether EORG's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for EORG of franchising its flagship restaurant brand to new cities.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Franchising lets EORG expand into new cities without bearing all the $750,000 capital or the property risk itself — franchisees fund their own sites while paying fees and royalties, multiplying the group's footprint and brand fame far faster than opening company-owned restaurants. This leverages the 78% 'very good' diner rating and the 57% repeat-visit base into markets where the group has no presence, and royalty streams are high-margin income that strengthens EORG's ability to service its $450,000 bank loan.

Disadvantage: Franchisees who cut corners on food quality or hygiene would damage the brand that 2.1% complaint rate and falling complaints (down from 3.4%) were built to protect; EORG could lose control of its two-for-one Tuesday execution and children's-dessert-Sunday promise across every franchised site. Legal setup, training, audit and support costs for the programme are real money against $31.60 average spend, and a failed franchisee in a new city could hand negative publicity and debt recovery to EORG precisely when kitchen absenteeism is already 12% and two head chefs have been poached.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to EORG's research, costs and franchise plans.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $11.05 and the 10.6% rise in protein, dairy and fresh produce input costs will affect EORG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): On EORG's $450,000 bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $3,375 a year in interest ($450,000 × 0.75% = $3,375), lifting fixed costs above $2,100,000. Higher rates may also deter borrowing by the very franchisees the $750,000 programme needs, and could make cautious diners trade down to cheaper eating out — eating-out spending grew just 2.9%. The direct cash impact is the smallest of the three, can be capped by fixing the loan rate, and unlike food costs never touches every one of the 260,000 meals EORG serves each year.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $11.05 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.65 ($11.05 − $10.40 = $0.65). The annual cost cannot be computed from the insert, because the number of hours paid at or near the minimum wage is not stated; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor overtakes the interest rise — it does so once EORG pays more than roughly 5,192 minimum-wage hours a year ($3,375 ÷ $0.65 ≈ 5,192), far below a plausible annual total for 120 staff across four restaurants plus weekend peaks (even a tiny slice of the workforce clears this). The rise also lands on a team already carrying 12% kitchen absenteeism, so resentment or rushed scheduling would cost more than the award itself; compliance is unavoidable, and personal retention may soften through menu voting and engagement.

Protein, dairy and fresh produce input costs (up 10.6% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names the core ingredients of a casual-dining plate. No share of the $9.50 variable cost is stated in the insert, so the correct bound runs from $0 to an upper bound built only on insert figures: applying the full 10.6% to the entire $9.50 gives at most about $1.01 per meal ($9.50 × 10.6% = $1.01), capping the damage at roughly $261,820 a year at 260,000 meals (260,000 × $1.01). The true figure sits between the bounds; inventing a food share would be fabrication, and any precise total would smuggle in an assumption the insert does not contain. What is certain is that every meal EORG serves — 260,000 a year — draws on these inputs, that menu prices are sticky against $24.50 with diners already trading down, and that a 10.6% squeeze on ingredients cannot be corrected by fixing a loan rate.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in protein, dairy and fresh produce input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 260,000 meals sold including future franchise volumes, is the steepest of the two cost-type percentage rises attached to the core product, and permits no financing fix. The 6.2% minimum wage increase is the second concern — material, unavoidable, and delicate given 12% kitchen absenteeism — while the 0.75 point interest rise costs exactly $3,375 a year and is the smallest, fixable by fixing the rate. EORG must respond with supplier renegotiation, menu engineering toward stable-priced dishes, tightening the 6.8% food-waste rate, and only selective price moves, so the franchise economics survive the ingredient squeeze while Meera Kapoor protects both margins and morale.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to EORG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on EORG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of EORG with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
